# Every command, and the same job in the window

VeilVoice is two programs over one engine. `veilvoice` is the command line and `veilvoice-gui` is the window, and they are not a menu bar and a wrapper around it: each has things the other does not, for reasons that are given below rather than left to be discovered.

This page is the whole of the command line, in the program's own order, with what each command is for in plain words and where the same job lives in the window. Every command also takes `--help`, which is the reference for its flags; this is the part that says what to reach for. The program's own `help` command prints those same pages, and is the one entry in its list with no section below, because there is nothing to say about it that this sentence has not.

**Nothing here reaches the network.** The one thing in VeilVoice that does is the window's check-for-updates button, and it is not a command.

## `veilvoice anonymise`

> De-identify an audio file and write a WAV

The main event, for a recording you already have. It reads almost any audio format, destroys the voiceprint, keeps every word, and seals the result so a veiled recording is not left lying about in the clear.

**In the window:** the **Anonymise file** tab, which is the same engine with the same defaults.

```bash
veilvoice anonymise interview.m4a -o clean.wav
```

## `veilvoice live`

> Scramble a microphone live, into a device or a virtual cable

Your microphone, veiled as you speak, into a virtual cable that other programs can use as their microphone. This is the one for a call, an interview or a stream.

**In the window:** the top half of the **Studio**, which starts the same session and draws the levels while it runs.

```bash
veilvoice live --output "CABLE Input (VB-Audio Virtual Cable)"
```

## `veilvoice record`

> Record yourself already veiled, straight into an encrypted file

Record yourself already veiled, straight into an encrypted file. The third case beside the two above: `live` keeps nothing and `anonymise` needs a recording that already exists in the clear. This never creates the original.

**In the window:** the bottom half of the **Studio**, which puts the take in the vault.

```bash
veilvoice record --seconds 120
```

## `veilvoice devices`

> List the audio devices this machine offers

What this machine offers as inputs and outputs, and which of them look like a virtual cable. Run it first when `live` cannot find the device you meant.

**In the window:** the two device pickers at the top of the **Studio**.

```bash
veilvoice devices
```

## `veilvoice clean`

> Strip identifying metadata from an audio or image file, in place

Strips identifying metadata out of an audio file or a photograph, in place: tags, timestamps, camera model, GPS. Veiling a voice and then sending a file that names your phone helps nobody.

**In the window:** the **strip metadata from the result** tick on the **Anonymise file** tab, which covers what VeilVoice writes; a photograph is this command.

```bash
veilvoice clean photo.jpg
```

## `veilvoice encrypt`

> Encrypt a file into a `.veil` container

Seals any file into a `.veil` container, under a passphrase or to somebody's public key. `anonymise` already seals what it writes, so this is for everything else: a note, an older recording, a key you want to move.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the window seals what it writes rather than offering a general encrypt button, so there is nothing here that this command does not do better.

```bash
veilvoice encrypt notes.wav --to friend.pub
```

## `veilvoice decrypt`

> Decrypt a `.veil` container

Opens a `.veil` container again, with the passphrase or the private key it was sealed to. This is how you get your WAV back after `anonymise`.

**In the window:** the **Browser**, which plays and exports what is in the vault without writing anything in the clear.

```bash
veilvoice decrypt clean.wav.veil -o clean.wav
```

## `veilvoice keygen`

> Generate a hybrid post-quantum key pair

Makes a hybrid post-quantum key pair, so somebody can seal a recording to you without either of you sharing a passphrase. The private half is itself stored encrypted.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the window accepts a `.pub` file and does not make one: a key pair is made once, deliberately, and belongs in the place you keep keys rather than behind a button.

```bash
veilvoice keygen
```

## `veilvoice guard`

> Record and check the integrity of VeilVoice's own files

Writes down what VeilVoice's own files should look like, then checks later that they still do. It notices changes and does not prevent them, and says so on every path through it.

**In the window:** the integrity report under the **Lock** tab, which reads the same record.

```bash
veilvoice guard init --sealed
```

## `veilvoice lock`

> Manage the application lock that guards the desktop app

The password for VeilVoice itself: set it, change it, remove it, or ask whether one is set and whether it is rate limited right now.

**In the window:** the **Lock** tab, which has the same four actions and the same account of what the lock is worth.

```bash
veilvoice lock set
```

## `veilvoice watch`

> Show which applications are using the microphone and camera

Which programs are holding your microphone and camera, with a log of starts and stops. The question this answers is whether something else is listening while you work.

**In the window:** the **Monitor** tab, plus the indicator that rides the header on every other tab.

```bash
veilvoice watch
```

## `veilvoice shred`

> Securely erase a file, then delete it. Irreversible

Overwrites a file's contents and then deletes it. For a recording that must not survive, with the honest limit printed every time: on flash storage the old blocks can survive every overwrite, and full-disk encryption is the real answer.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: there is no button for this on purpose. It cannot be undone, and a one-click irreversible delete beside a list of recordings is an accident waiting to be made.

```bash
veilvoice shred secret.wav
```

## `veilvoice info`

> Show version and build information

Version, build and what this copy can do on this machine. The first thing to paste into a bug report.

**In the window:** the **About** tab, which shows the same information and the paths in use.

```bash
veilvoice info
```

## `veilvoice accel`

> The graphics hardware here, and what it is good for

What graphics hardware is here and what it is good for, which decides how fast a render goes and whether the window draws on the GPU.

**In the window:** the graphics line on the **About** tab, taken from the driver that actually drew the window.

```bash
veilvoice accel
```

## `veilvoice gui`

> Open the desktop application

Opens the desktop application. Exactly the same as running `veilvoice-gui`, and it exists so that somebody who has only met the command line does not have to know there are two programs.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: this command *is* the window.

```bash
veilvoice gui
```

## `veilvoice install`

> Copy VeilVoice somewhere the system can find it, and add it to PATH

Copies VeilVoice somewhere the system can find it and adds it to your PATH, so `veilvoice` works from any directory. Running from the folder you unpacked is a supported choice, not a lesser one.

**In the window:** the **Install** tab, which an installed copy does not show, because a program offering to install itself when it already is tells you something untrue.

```bash
veilvoice install
```

## `veilvoice uninstall`

> Undo what `install` did: the PATH entry, the uninstall entry, and the installed copy

Undoes exactly what `install` did: the copy, the PATH entry and the uninstall entry. It does not touch your settings, your app lock or your recordings.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the window has no uninstall button: a program's own interface is the wrong place to remove it from, and on Windows the platform's own entry is where people look.

```bash
veilvoice uninstall
```

## `veilvoice policy`

> Settings fixed so the interface cannot turn them off

Settings fixed so the interface cannot turn them off, for a machine somebody else is responsible for. Every setting a policy can reach makes VeilVoice stricter; there is no room in the format for one that loosens it.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: a policy the interface could switch off would not be a policy. The window shows what is in force and greys out what the policy has decided.

```bash
veilvoice policy status
```

## `veilvoice mandate`

> The two things VeilVoice insists on, unless you say otherwise

The two things VeilVoice insists on unless you say otherwise: a password for itself, and encryption for every recording. This is the one place that can make it less strict, for your own machine, and every change is written down with its date.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: relaxing a requirement is a decision with a date on it rather than a tick box, so it is asked for deliberately at a terminal.

```bash
veilvoice mandate status
```

## `veilvoice conversation`

> A recording with several people in it: a voice each, and subtitles

A recording with several people in it: a voice each, subtitles, and every voiceprint destroyed just as thoroughly. You say who is talking, in a plan file, because guessing would merge two people or invent a third.

**In the window:** the **Group** tab, which is the same plan built by pointing and clicking.

```bash
veilvoice conversation render plan.toml -o out.wav
```

## `veilvoice capture`

> Which screen recorders are running, and which you meant to run

Which screen recorders are running, and where to point Discord, Signal, Telegram and the rest so your voice goes through VeilVoice first. It tells you once and then stops telling you if you say you meant it.

**In the window:** the recorder list on the **Monitor** tab.

```bash
veilvoice capture status
```

## `veilvoice decoy`

> A second passphrase that opens an empty VeilVoice, and its limits

A second passphrase that opens an empty VeilVoice, for complying with somebody standing over you. It does not give you deniability, since this feature is documented and the program is open source, and no passphrase destroys anything.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: a decoy passphrase offered by the interface is not a decoy. The **Browser** can fill the folder with decoy vaults, which is the other half of the same idea.

```bash
veilvoice decoy
```

## `veilvoice failsafe`

> The safety catch: what it watches for, and what it cannot do

The safety catch: it notices when another program picks up a real microphone while you are being veiled, which is the accident where a headset is plugged in and the call quietly switches over. It notices within about a second and cannot prevent it, and prints the difference every time.

**In the window:** always on while the **Studio** is veiling, and reported there.

```bash
veilvoice failsafe
```

## `veilvoice privilege`

> What VeilVoice is running with, and what that lets it see

What VeilVoice is running with and what that lets it see. The monitoring features see further as an administrator; it never raises its own privileges or asks for a password, and prints the command to run it the other way.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the window reports what it can and cannot see on the **Monitor** tab rather than asking to be trusted with more.

```bash
veilvoice privilege
```

## `veilvoice appctl`

> Learn what normally runs here, then notice what does not

Learn what normally runs on this machine, then notice what does not. Run `learn` for a few days of ordinary work, close the baseline, and `check` afterwards. It blocks nothing and cannot: it is a way of noticing.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: a baseline is built over days from a terminal, and a window that had to stay open for it would be the wrong shape for the job.

```bash
veilvoice appctl check
```

## `veilvoice input`

> What running programs can see your keyboard and mouse

Which running programs are *able* to see your keyboard and mouse: remote-support tools, macro recorders, password managers, screen readers. It cannot tell you whether anything is logging you, and nothing can, and it says that with every result.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the same list would need the same paragraph beside it, and the honest place for a result that cannot be a verdict is a terminal somebody asked.

```bash
veilvoice input look
```

## `veilvoice sentry`

> Canaries, and how fast a folder is changing

Two early warnings that something is going through your files: a canary file nothing should ever touch, and a baseline that says how fast a folder is changing. Neither stops anything and neither names the program responsible.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: planting a canary is a change to a folder you own, asked for once from a terminal rather than offered in a panel.

```bash
veilvoice sentry plant ~/Recordings
```

## `veilvoice companions`

> Optional third-party software VeilVoice works with, and whether this machine already has it

The optional third-party software VeilVoice works with, whether this machine already has it, and how to get it. Nothing proprietary is ever installed without you agreeing to its licence.

**In the window:** the companion list on the **About** tab, which installs with the same confirmation, cancel and resume.

```bash
veilvoice companions
```

## `veilvoice verify`

> Check a download, and what does the checking

Checks a download against the signed hash list, and says what did the checking. The signing key is compiled into this binary, so a download that brings its own key and its own signature cannot vouch for itself.

**In the window:** the **Verify** tab, which takes the files by drag and drop and can ask your own GnuPG the same question.

```bash
veilvoice verify file veilvoice.tar.gz --sums SHA256SUMS --sig SHA256SUMS.asc
```

## `veilvoice video`

> Turn a veiled recording into a video with a black picture

Turns a veiled recording into a video with a black picture, for posting somewhere that will not accept an audio file. Needs ffmpeg, which VeilVoice does not ship and will not install: it prints the exact command when the tool is missing.

**In the window:** the export button in the **Browser**, which writes the same file from the vault.

```bash
veilvoice video clean.wav -o clean.mp4
```

## `veilvoice import`

> Take the sound out of a recording made somewhere else

Pulls the audio out of a recording made somewhere else, such as anything OBS writes, into a WAV that `anonymise` can take. Needs ffmpeg, with the same refusal as above.

**In the window:** the **Anonymise file** tab reads audio formats directly; a video container is this command first.

```bash
veilvoice import stream.mkv -o stream.wav
```

## `veilvoice volumes`

> Encrypted volumes this machine has: Cryptomator and VeraCrypt

Which encrypted volumes this machine has, Cryptomator and VeraCrypt, and which are mounted right now. It never opens, closes or unlocks anything and never asks for a volume password: mounting your storage is your act, in the tool you chose.

**In the window:** nothing, and that is deliberate: the window writes into whatever folder you give it, mounted volume or not, and deliberately does not learn how to mount things.

```bash
veilvoice volumes
```
